Fishing Rights allocation fiasco

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
Fishing rights have been allocated for the next 15 years and the appeals process has begun. It appears that the Tuna Pole sector has had the most new entrants and 70% of the former rights holders who were active and have boats have not been granted rights. That has a massive impact- the people they employ are sitting at home for the last two months. Normally they extend the rights to fish while they undergo the new allocations and the appeals process. The whole FRAP process has been delayed since 2020 due to COVID and a social economic impact assessment. The people who have “lost” rights are likely to regain them in the appeals process but in the mean time they are fishing on other people quotas and paying R1.20 per kilo. If the DEFF had just extended the current the rights which they had done since 2020 until the appeals process was done and then people would be kept in the water and families fed

Summary:
In the 1st few weeks there was major horse trading going on – one guy got 21 calls within the first day to ask if he wanted to fish their quotas when rights were allocated, but it comes at a price- they will have to pay R1 on every kg of fish caught and then they may have to pay the more to have the fish offloaded. Its peak tuna fishing time and they can easily catch 25 tons in the 2 months they grounded loosing massively and with a 30 million rand investment in a boat you are forced to take it.
Many of the Tuna quotas were issued to Squid boats in PE and there is no tuna off PE so they are getting the grounded fishing boats to fish their quotas- is been argued this is BEEE fronting
Once rights have been issued they cant be removed and the people that have been excluded will probably get their rights back after the which means there will be 150 boats at sea and this probably will lead to over fishing because its an effort based industry, there were 70 active boats, there are 60 new entrants.



Further information:
Gary Kingma comes from a very long line of fishermen and is one of the top tuna pole fishermen in terms of what he catches - he was excluded because his Tax Clearance certificate expired- they only are issued for 3 months- the application process began in December- so he will have to fish on somebody else’s right and pay per kilogram- what that means is the boat owners costs are not, inevitably that means fishermen get paid less and some paper quota holder is getting rich and never going to sea. It also leads to illegal fishing because you have to keep fishing to cover your costs
In the Hake Long line sector which is raising lots of questions and possibly an example of fronting is a boat called Monnickendam. It hasn’t gone to sea for many years and is worth about 500k – it has 6 rights holders who have been issued quotas on this boat- the total quotas amounts to 4.0444 of the percentage allocated- 4% of 9000 tons at approx R12/kg after all costs before tax amounts to roughly R4.5 mill per year for 15yrs. What they will do is sell those rights at R9 a kilogram to people who do have boats. Mike Stowe has resigned as the director of the company that owns Monnikedam. On Windeed the director is listed as Lefang Phumeza address is 2565 KANANA STREET, MASIPHUMELELE, MASIPHUMELELE, WESTERN CAPE, 7975 and Qogi Ayazola W128, Wetlands, Masiphumelele. Tomorrow I will go on a recce to these address and see what checks out

Monnikendam last Hull certificate expired in 2018 and hasn’t been picked up on the Maritime tracking device and locals in Hout Bay harbour say that vessel hasn’t been to sea in years- yet they were awarded a huge right- how does this process work
The DEFF said they would not allocate right to Sport recreation vessels got Tuna pole rights like Monish and Mustang- how will they fulfil their quotas



Extra Budget Items:
Extra overnight stay- The fishing boats come in at midnight to offload at 1st light and they are our main case study and Claire needs to be on the dock. she will have to fly in the night before

Script:


Script: It’s an ungodly hour to be offloading these yellowfin tuna - but the next flight to Spain, is just hours away, and the fresh tuna market is thriving.
LINK “ This is the hard face of fishing – its 4 o'clock in the morning and these men have been out at sea for the last 5 days hauling in massive tuna out of the ocean by hand- but their livelyhood hangs in the balance
Script: It’s the height of tuna season, and they need to spend every possible day at sea, before the tuna migrate, leaving our waters around June. Mike Smith, is chair of the large pelagic and SMME association.
Upsound on the dock - Mike” 25 years ago I couldn’t give this fish away we used to sell it for R3 a kilo but thanks to the cooking channels I don’t know if you remember Floyd with his glass of wine
Claire Yeees with a glass
Script: Now their problem is the Department of Forestry Fisheries and Environment, who regulate the industry. They decide who can and cannot catch fish, and how much- known as the Fishing Rights Application Process or FRAP and it’s always highly contested.
Claire: let's talk about the right's allocation process. It seems like the tuna pole, um, sector has been hardest hit.
Mike: you‘re hundred percent right 00:03:39:23 the people who should be offloading fish today are tied up and unable to work. And we don't know how long it's going to take before they can get back to sea.
Script: 9 sectors within the commercial fishing industry have just been reallocated - big companies like Oceana and I&J, are in Hake and Deep sea trawl. The smaller players are in Tuna-pole running their own businesses, with small crews.
Script: Walter has been fishing since he was 12, taught by his uncles. He’s paying off a R7 million boat, and is exactly the kind of person the Department said they wanted to create access for. He applied for a tuna pole right for the 1st time this year
LINK: Walters family have been fishing for other people for generations, but this year was supposed to be different he was hoping to get fishing rights so that he could make real money and be the master of his own destiny
Script But despite his investment, he was unsuccessful
Claire: And what did that feel like?
Walter: Joh It felt like my whole world was coming down on me, it still feels like my whole world is coming down, because I need to pay this vessel, if I don't get on sea in the next year, month or two, I'm going to be screwed. I can lose everything.
LINK This is the equivalent of the high stakes gambling in the fishing industry rights have just been allocated for the next 15 years – companies have spent millions investing in new boats in the hopes of landing lucrative quotas but the entire process has been mired in controversy
Script: Most graphically illustrated here
LINK- how did a boat like this that hasn’t been to sea in years get a tuna right?
Script: And it’s not the only example- there many- did the Department apply its mind- or are there other issues at play. Why are 70% of the working tuna pole boats denied rights?
Claire: So when last did you go to sea? When did you last go out fishing
Gary: Its a month and a half ago. And I'm dying inside. And if I see another red robot, I'm going to drive it over with my old rusty bakkie.
Script: Gary Kingma, viewed as one of the top tuna pole fishermen – legendary for going out to sea in extreme weather with 18 men onboard, was denied a right.
Claire:. What has the process been like?
Gary: Oh, it's been an absolute nightmare, 00:00:59:29…... It doesn't make any sense to us because as fishermen we catch fish, and the more fish you catch, the better fisherman you are. But we don't seem to be scored on that in any way. It's got more to do with a whole lot of like different factors that industry has imposed on us and doesn't really make sense in our world.
Script: Rights allocation is a lengthy technical process that should have begun in 2018 and awarded in 2020- but after countless delays, the process only started in October last year
Mike “And when this rights allocation process came out, …. they were trying to rush everything to get it finished by the end of last year, we knew the department would never get it right in the time period, but they keep just saying, you have to get it done, you have to get it done. 00:04:13:06 This happens every single rights allocation process. We don't move forward. We don't learn from years past. We actually getting worse each time round.
Script: And for the 1st time it was done entirely online- but it appears it wasn’t tested before it went live. The forms kept changing right up until the closing date. Data and applications entered went missing, people who had registered were simply not on the system. The questions were so complex and inappropriate, for the majority of applicants, says Shaheen Muller.
Shaheen The online system just failed. It was introduced in a matter of days without any pre-planning, no consultation with industry. Not a single right holder knew what to expect when this process came live – it did not perhaps prejudice a large corporation with the resources but it harmed our traditional line fishers who just could not work this complicated IT system.
Claire Also wasn't it insecure like information that was loaded could be viewed by other people
Shaheen. I've got video evidence of me using my client's credentials and log in passwords and landing on a third parties application, which I could have amended, you know, deleted information, etc., at will. And we don't know who did that or who suffered those consequences.
Script: Walter couldn’t afford lawyers at R100 000 to fill in his application
Walter most of the questions on that thing was really for me, it was hectic, when we had in the nights of not sleeping because we weren't worried. What if we don't get in and we didn't get anything. We were struggling with stuff.
Claire: So the rights were going to allocated in 28 days. How many applications were - needed to be assessed and was that a realistic number
Shaheen: 2800 applications were actually received across the nine fishing sectors. There was no way that the a human being, …could have conceivably received, evaluated, scored and made decisions on those numbers of applications in that time frame
Script: The Department acknowledged what they called glitches, and after an outcry from the fishermen,extended the deadline. Then said an independent observer deemed the process free, fair and transparent. Some fishermen feel otherwise - How did most of the tuna rights get awarded to new people who don't even have boats in Cape Town, where tuna are caught from
Mike: new entrants into the fishery appear to be at face value, just pure paper quota holders. So they don't have the means to operate. They don't have the vessels. They don't have the knowledge and rights were now starting to be traded very quickly, as an example in 24 hours, one person with the telephone managed to find 21 different fishing rights that he could operate on. It started to highlight something the Department has tried and professed to be wanting to get rid of.
Script: Allegations of corruption and fronting abound -rights holders sit back and rake in the money from the fishermen, who have to pay them per kilo of fish they catch. Yet they still carry the hard costs of repairs, new boats, and crew.
Gary how come the guy next door to me who hasn't even been to sea he gets allocated a quota? …., it's literally taken the fishermen out of fishing, you know?- it's a gross mismanagement and injustice to the fishermen and the communities themselves
Script: It’s management decision like they can fish for nearly two years on a permit extension, while the department gets their house in order and then suddenly at the height of tuna season, they must stop
Mike: a decent exemption literally to the end of 2022 it would have given this whole FRAP process time to sort itself out, and there would have been no disruption to the industry at all, no jobs lost.
Claire: It sounds like the department. Doesn't really understand the nuances of this industry.
Mike: Sadly, I don't think that they have the vaguest idea how the industry operates, management at a senior level at DEFF, that is is one of our biggest challenges.
LINK We asked the Department of Forestry Fisheries and Environment for an interview in February but they declined stating the rights allocation process was still underway - now the rights have been allocated
Script: they said the appeal process is underway and anyone who is dissatisfied has till the 29 May to do so - and historically, that outcome takes years
Claire: what is the feeling now with your clients? This appeal process
Shaheen: there are some decisions that are appealable. The ones that are just blatantly exclusionary, just unlawful. On the other hand, they are those applications and those unfortunately outnumber the appealable ones, …this is the end of the line for them, If we don't go to court
Script: Walter feels broken, he’s back working others permits, paying them for every kilo of fish he catches
Walter: But 15 years from now, what age am I going to be to apply then for a permit, almost 60 years old…. I don't want to go work for someone again…….

metadata.Summary: In the 1st few weeks there was major horse trading going on – one guy got 21 calls within the first day to ask if he wanted to fish their quotas when rights were allocated, but it comes at a price- they will have to pay R1 on every kg of fish caught and then they may have to pay the more to have the fish offloaded. Its peak tuna fishing time and they can easily catch 25 tons in the 2 months they grounded loosing massively and with a 30 million rand investment in a boat you are forced to take it. Many of the Tuna quotas were issued to Squid boats in PE and there is no tuna off PE so they are getting the grounded fishing boats to fish their quotas- is been argued this is BEEE fronting Once rights have been issued they cant be removed and the people that have been excluded will probably get their rights back after the which means there will be 150 boats at sea and this probably will lead to over fishing because its an effort based industry, there were 70 active boats, there are 60 new entrants.
metadata.Further information: Gary Kingma comes from a very long line of fishermen and is one of the top tuna pole fishermen in terms of what he catches - he was excluded because his Tax Clearance certificate expired- they only are issued for 3 months- the application process began in December- so he will have to fish on somebody else’s right and pay per kilogram- what that means is the boat owners costs are not, inevitably that means fishermen get paid less and some paper quota holder is getting rich and never going to sea. It also leads to illegal fishing because you have to keep fishing to cover your costs In the Hake Long line sector which is raising lots of questions and possibly an example of fronting is a boat called Monnickendam. It hasn’t gone to sea for many years and is worth about 500k – it has 6 rights holders who have been issued quotas on this boat- the total quotas amounts to 4.0444 of the percentage allocated- 4% of 9000 tons at approx R12/kg after all costs before tax amounts to roughly R4.5 mill per year for 15yrs. What they will do is sell those rights at R9 a kilogram to people who do have boats. Mike Stowe has resigned as the director of the company that owns Monnikedam. On Windeed the director is listed as Lefang Phumeza address is 2565 KANANA STREET, MASIPHUMELELE, MASIPHUMELELE, WESTERN CAPE, 7975 and Qogi Ayazola W128, Wetlands, Masiphumelele. Tomorrow I will go on a recce to these address and see what checks out Monnikendam last Hull certificate expired in 2018 and hasn’t been picked up on the Maritime tracking device and locals in Hout Bay harbour say that vessel hasn’t been to sea in years- yet they were awarded a huge right- how does this process work The DEFF said they would not allocate right to Sport recreation vessels got Tuna pole rights like Monish and Mustang- how will they fulfil their quotas
